(Co-located with ISMB 2026 ) | Online Participation Available Theme of ICBO 2026 ¶ The International Conference on Biological and Biomedical Ontology (ICBO) is a premier annual conference series covering the development and application of ontologies for biological and medical domains. The emergence of Generative AI (GenAI) is fundamentally altering the landscape of biomedical research, knowledge integration, and scientific communication. However, the rapid acceleration of data generation does not inherently lead to improved scientific understanding. As AI systems increasingly mediate the synthesis of knowledge, the requirements for semantic rigor, ontological grounding, and data trustworthiness become more paramount. ICBO 2026 invites contributions exploring the critical role of ontologies and semantic technologies (including formal semantics based Knowledge Graph) in developing trustworthy, interpretable, and AI-ready ecosystems. We welcome research across the domains of biology, medicine, health, behavioral science, environmental health, and food systems. While GenAI offers powerful capabilities for data processing and synthesis, it serves as a complement to, not a replacement for, formal semantics, logical consistency, and community-curated knowledge structures. This year's focus extends to how AI and large language models can revolutionize ontology studies, enhancing literature mining, meta-analysis, and complex data interpretation. docs.text: Call for Submissions ¶ ICBO 2026 invites contributions exploring the critical role of ontologies and semantic technologies in developing trustworthy, interpretable, and AI-ready ecosystems. Original research, system descriptions, and position papers are invited addressing the following challenges. Topics of Interest ¶ 1. Ontological Foundations for Trustworthy AI ¶ Methods for grounding Large Language Models (LLMs) in formal ontologies Advancements in neuro-symbolic AI and explainable AI (XAI) Ensuring logical consistency in AI-mediated knowledge discovery 2. Semantic Modeling and Bounding of GenAI ¶ Ontology-driven validation of generative outputs Semantic approaches to hallucination detection and mitigation Integration of Knowledge Graphs (KGs) with generative workflows 3. Domain-Specific Applications in Biomedical Research ¶ Practical implementations across core domains: Life Sciences: Molecular biology, genomics, and proteomics discovery Clinical & Public Health: Heterogeneous data integration for epidemiology and health informatics Wellness & Behavior: Frameworks for mental health, physical wellness, environmental health, and behavioral science Global Systems: Food safety, agricultural systems, and environmental sustainability 4. AI-Readiness and Semantic Infrastructure ¶ Defining and benchmarking "AI-readiness" for datasets and ontologies Governance, sustainability, and community standards evolution Semantic metadata's role in model training and fine-tuning 5. FAIR Principles in the Era of GenAI ¶ Evaluating FAIR principles sufficiency for machine-actionable data Provenance, traceability, and reproducibility in AI-integrated pipelines 6. Practical and Theoretical Perspectives ¶ Distinctions between Semantics and Ontology in GenAI contexts The future of biocuration and manual knowledge engineering ICBO Conference Proceeding Publication Requirements ¶ All conference submissions (excluding posters and software demo submissions) accepted will be published in the CEUR Workshop Proceedings as part of the new IAOA series . An example from a past conference can be seen here . In order for this to happen, the following requirements must be satisfied: All submissions should be in Adobe Portable Document Format (PDF) and should follow the CEUR-Template-1col-ICBO2026.odt file, single column. The template in OverLeaf (LaTeX) version is available here . Please make a copy of the project to edit in your own Overleaf accounts. Ensure that the conference name, date, and place, and email addresses and ORCIDs of all authors are added to the footnote on the lower left of the first page. Note that the template (.odt version) provided in the link above already includes the standardized copyright footer for ICBO 2026 with the conference name and date. You only need to fill in the EMAIL and ORCID information for each author. All papers for ICBO MUST have an accompanying signed Author Agreement to Publish a Contribution as Open-Access on CEUR-WS.org prepared by the corresponding author. Please download one of the ICBO 2026 customized forms below: AUTHOR-AGREEMENT (NTP) : Authors shall use this form if they included no copyrighted third party material in their paper text (or accompanying sources, datasets). This is the right variant in most cases. AUTHOR-AGREEMENT (TP) : Authors shall use this form if they did include copyrighted third party material in their paper or accompanying material. They must then also attach a copy of the permission by the third party to use this material in the signed author agreement! The CEURART template contains specific instructions on certain mandatory elements such as the Declaration on Generative AI. Make sure that all paper PDFs follow the template's instructions. Authors should also adhere to the CEUR-WS Policy on AI-Assisting Tools . Fill in the fields on the AUTHOR-AGREEMENT form, print it out, sign it in ink (by hand), then scan or photograph the form and both upload it on the ICBO 2026 Submission Portal and send it to: ontology.world@gmail.com with a subject heading that reads "Author Agreement for submission PAPER [PAPER-ID]". Please note that CEUR strictly requires a hand-written wet-ink signature on a printed version of the agreement by the corresponding author (acting on behalf of all co-authors). Do NOT digitally sign the pdf, as CEUR-WS.org will not accept it. CEUR-WS.org allows an alternative method to provide a signature if you are unable to print the form, as shown here . Update your camera-ready paper on the official submission portal. Call for Workshop & Tutorial Proposals ¶ Submission deadline: March 30, 2026. Notification: April 6, 2026. Workshop submission — one pager including title, organizers names and contacts, workshop description, duration. Submit via: ICBO 2026 Submission Portal Contact: Boonserm (Serm) Kulvatunyou — boonserm.kulvatunyou@nist.gov Call for Direct-to-Journal Track Papers ¶ Direct-to-journal track submission deadline: April 15, 2026. Notification: June 1, 2026. In collaboration with the Journal of Biomedical Semantics (JBMS) . Papers submitted to the International Conference on Biological and Biomedical Ontology track at the Journal of Biomedical Semantics will be published immediately after acceptance and presented in the annual conference following acceptance. The new ICBO Thematic Series at the JBMS is soliciting submissions of novel (not previously published nor concurrently submitted) research papers in the areas of ontology design, development, evaluation and use, ontology interoperability, knowledge graphs, ontology-driven intelligent systems, ontologies for explainable AI, and the application of ontologies to biological and biomedical problems, across the full range of life sciences. In addition, we would like to invite contributions showcasing methods for ontology-based research, including statistical methods, tool support for ontologies and semantic technologies including for the annotation of data, visualisation, analysis, and related applications, and contributions addressing the challenges associated with working with multiple ontologies at the same time, including ontology alignment and matching. Submissions are welcome from a broad range of approaches to ontology building and use. More information can be found at https://link.springer.com/collections/gagejcafef . Submission: The submission guidelines will follow the journal's submission requirements — see Journal of Biomedical Semantics submission guidelines . Contact: Sunghwan Kim Call for ICBO Conference Papers ¶ Conference paper submission deadline: May 1, 2026. Notification: June 1, 2026. The following paper categories are welcome: Full Research Papers ¶ 8–12 pages (including references). Short Papers ¶ Up to 7 pages (including references). Posters & Software Demos ¶ Presentations of emerging tools, software systems, and early-stage concepts. For each paper accepted, at least one author must register. Submission link: ICBO 2026 Submission Portal Call for Posters & Software Demos ¶ Submission deadline: June 1, 2026 June 12, 2026 (Extended!) . Notification: June 15, 2026. Posters and software demos are an opportunity to present emerging tools, software systems, and early-stage research concepts. Submissions should include a brief description of the work, its relevance to the conference themes, and (for software demos) a description of the system to be demonstrated. Accepted abstracts are listed on the Poster Abstracts page. Submission link: ICBO 2026 Submission Portal Important Dates ¶ Mark Your Calendar The main conference takes place July 15–17, 2026 . Please note the submission deadlines below. Track Submission Deadline Acceptance Notification Workshop & Tutorial Proposals March 30, 2026 April 6, 2026 Direct-to-Journal Track April 15, 2026 June 1, 2026 Main Conference Papers May 1, 2026 June 1, 2026 Posters & Software Demos June 1, 2026 June 12, 2026 (Extended!) June 15, 2026 Program Committee ¶ Program Committee Coordination: Qian Zhu (NIH) Program committee members will be announced soon. Acknowledgment ¶ The Microsoft CMT service was used for managing the peer-reviewing process for this conference. This service was provided for free by Microsoft and they bore all expenses, including costs for Azure cloud services as well as for software development and support. Contact Information ¶ Please direct all questions to Asiyah Yu Lin — ontology.world@gmail.com

docs.text: Poster & Software Demo Abstracts ¶ July 15–17, 2026 | Columbia Ballroom, Washington Hilton, Washington D.C. Accepted posters and software demos will be presented during the poster and demo recesses on Day 1 (10:00 – 11:00 AM and 4:00 – 4:40 PM) and Day 2 (10:00 – 11:00 AM). See the Conference Agenda for the full schedule. Accepted Abstracts ¶ Poster Cell Line Ontology in 2026 ¶ Jie Zheng, Stella Liao, Abigail Samuelson, Yongqun He University of Michigan Medical School, Ann Arbor, MI, USA The Cell Line Ontology (CLO), an OBO Foundry member initiated in 2010, contains more than 43,000 terms standardizing the representation of cell lines from ATCC, HyperCLDB, and other repositories. After a pause in active development, CLO development resumed in 2026 and several major issues were identified and resolved: 609 ROBOT-reported errors (duplicate labels, duplicate definitions, and multiple definitions), imported terms that had been deprecated or replaced in their source ontologies, and inconsistent application of the cell line cell design pattern. CLO was also realigned from BFO to the Core Ontology for Biology and Biomedicine (COB) to strengthen interoperability, and a Makefile-based release workflow using OntoFox and ROBOT templates was implemented. These updates support richer queries over cell lines by derived cell type, anatomical structure, source organism, disease model, and repository. Keywords: ontology, Cell Line Ontology, cell line Read full abstract (PDF) Software Demo CellCards 2.0: An Ontology-Driven Platform for Anatomically Contextualized Cell and Cell Line Knowledge Integration ¶ Feng-Yu Yeh, Mary Czelusniak, Stella Liao, Jie Zheng, William D. Duncan, Alexander D. Diehl, Bruce W. Herr II, Katy Börner, Yongqun He University of Michigan; University of Florida College of Dentistry; NF/SG VAHS; University at Buffalo; Indiana University CellCards is an ontology-driven knowledgebase for the standardized characterization of cell types. Because identical cell types can exhibit distinct molecular and functional profiles across tissues, CellCards 2.0 maps Cell Ontology (CL) identifiers to multiple UBERON anatomical contexts, enabling tissue-specific disambiguation of primary cells, and adds over 30,000 immortalized cell lines represented through the Cell Line Ontology (CLO). The platform integrates HuBMAP ASCT+B tables and Functional Tissue Unit reference models, ingests ontology-linked metadata from over 160,000 Cellosaurus records, and retrieves CL and CLO information via Ontobee SPARQL queries. The demo showcases tissue-aware cell exploration, ontology-linked biomarker integration, and semantic disambiguation workflows across multi-source biomedical datasets. Keywords: Cell Ontology; Cell Line Ontology; semantic integration; HuBMAP; biomedical ontologies Read full abstract (PDF) cellcards.org Poster Connecting Neural Circuit Biotypes to Pharmacogenomics: An OWL 2 DL Ontology Extension for Precision Psychiatry Decision Support ¶ Lucas Wozniak, Atul Chaudhari, Chuyi Zhang, Lauren Hamilton Depression and anxiety disorders exhibit substantial biological heterogeneity, yet no existing system provides a unified, computable representation linking neural circuit biotype classification to pharmacogenomics safety constraints for antidepressant prescribing. This work presents a confidence-qualified neural phenotype ontology joining the two domains through an OWL 2 DL knowledge architecture, a Bayesian network for biotype inference, and a pharmacogenomics clinical decision support module. The ontology aligns to BFO 2020 and bridges via SKOS to UBERON, HPO, the Cognitive Atlas, and SNOMED CT, with accompanying SSSOM mapping tables; it validates as OWL 2 DL-conformant with zero ROBOT errors. An HL7 CDS Hooks 2.0 service combines SPARQL-queried drug–gene relationships, CPIC Activity Score rules, and FHIR Genomics Reporting IG v3.0.0 genotype data to generate real-time prescribing alerts, maintaining a strict separation between ontology vocabulary, curated knowledge base, and procedural rule engine. Read full abstract (PDF) Demo Poster Enabling Cross-Domain Semantic Data Integration with an RDF Representation of RefChem ¶ Qingliang Li, Sunghwan Kim, Paul Thiessen, Jian Zhang, Tiejun Cheng, Asta Gindulyte, Siqian He, Evan Bolton National Center for Biotechnology Information, National Library of Medicine, NIH, Bethesda, MD, USA Chemical entity integration across heterogeneous biomedical resources remains a persistent challenge, since even authoritative sources disagree over whether two representations refer to the same entity — formaldehyde as a gas versus formalin as an aqueous solution, or active pharmaceutical ingredients versus their salt forms. RefChem, the PubChem Reference Collection, disambiguates and semantically organizes chemical substances using standardized structures, names, and identifiers. This work presents an RDF-based representation of RefChem that captures substance identity, structural relationships, naming types, associations, and variants, enabling formal semantic integration within PubChemRDF and across external resources such as drugs, toxicology data, biological assays, literature, and patents, and advancing the interoperability and FAIRness of chemical data. Read full abstract (PDF) Poster Semantic Mapping of Psychological Assessment Questions to BERTopic-Derived Solitude-Related Concepts Using SciBERT Embeddings ¶ B. Damayanthi Jesudas, Jérémy Ravenel, Maxime Jublou, Sam Smith, Feng-Yu Yeh, Jie Zheng, Yongqun He, Regina Hurley, Julie C. Bowker, Hollen N. Reischer, John Beverley, William D. Duncan University of Florida; NF/SG VAHS; University at Buffalo; University of Michigan Medical School; NaasAI, Inc. Part of the Promoting Healthy Aging through Semantic Enrichment of Solitude Research (PHASES) project, this study extends prior BERTopic modeling of The Handbook of Solitude by semantically linking psychological assessment questions to BERTopic-derived topic representations using SciBERT embeddings. Questions drawn from the UCLA Loneliness Scale, Differential Loneliness Scale, Inventory of Interpersonal Problems, and Subjective Happiness and Loneliness Scales were encoded alongside topic summaries, and cosine similarity identified the five most semantically similar topics per question. The framework captures relationships beyond keyword overlap and surfaces candidate psychological constructs for ontology development, while demonstrating that subject matter expert review remains necessary to separate genuinely relevant concepts from semantically related but conceptually irrelevant topics. Keywords: SciBERT; BERTopic; semantic similarity; psychological assessment; solitude; ontology development Read full abstract (PDF) Project website Source code Poster Tracking Usage of Ontologies in the Translational Science Ecosystem ¶ Sebastian Duesing, Fabrício Rodrigues, Barry Smith Department of Philosophy, University at Buffalo, Amherst, NY, USA Translational research projects use ontologies to annotate, analyze, and harmonize diversely formatted data, and both the ontologies and the projects benefit when developers understand how their ontologies are used. At present, however, it is almost impossible for open-source ontology development teams to identify where their ontologies are being used outside their own laboratories. Ontology browsers such as Ontobee and the Ontology Lookup Service expose inter-ontology dependencies, but comparable visibility into downstream project use does not exist. The authors propose a registry of ontology usage in translational research (ROUTR) to collect and disseminate information about how clinical translational science projects use and depend on ontologies. Keywords: ontology, ontology usage, clinical translational science, database Read full abstract (PDF) Poster Using MedGen to Assign Clinical Categories to Tests and Utilize the Disease Categories as a Search Criterion for Tests in the NIH Genetic Testing Registry (GTR®) ¶ Thilakam Venkatapathi, Adriana Malheiro, Megan Kane, Marilu Hoeppner, Baoshan Gu, George Zhou, Doug Hoffman, Sahithi Punyasamudram, Brandi Kattman National Center for Biotechnology Information, National Library of Medicine, NIH, Bethesda, MD, USA MedGen integrates clinically relevant and sometimes orthogonal ontologies and vocabularies — including HPO, Mondo, OrphaNet, a UMLS subset, OMIM, PharmGKB, GeneReviews, and GARD — under one resource, mapping equivalent concepts to a single MedGen record and routing automated-pipeline discrepancies to curators for review. To help clinicians select suitable tests in the NIH Genetic Testing Registry , this work assigns broad clinical specialty labels to tests: higher-level HPO and Mondo nodes are matched to each clinical category label, descendants inherit that label, and the labels collected across a test's indicated diseases are scored by how frequently they are represented in order to prioritize display. The resulting clinical categories now power retrieval of tests by broad clinical category in GTR's advanced search. Read full abstract (PDF) Contact Information ¶ Please direct all questions to Asiyah Yu Lin — ontology.world@gmail.com
